What I learned from Arkham's talk and what we can apply at Revyse

Talk by Rubén Escalante Chan (Sr. Software Engineer) and Raúl Mosqueda (AI Researcher), Arkham Technologies

Ana Castellanos

Who is Arkham

  • Arkham Technologies: "Operational AI Platform for the modern enterprise".
  • Unifies company data, trusted metrics and AI models adapted to each operation.
  • Data infrastructure & analytics · Palo Alto, CA, with a team in Mexico City.
  • Public case: retail project with Circle K in Mexico.
  • Speakers: Rubén Escalante Chan, Sr. Software Engineer · Raúl Mosqueda, AI Researcher.

Sources: arkham.tech, Arkham Technologies on LinkedIn, thunder.mx

The core idea

  • Arkham no longer "writes code": its engineering team builds product with an agent harness.
  • Engineers are still the ones making the decisions.
  • Everything starts with a good spec.

Scope, interfaces and criteria

1 · Spec Driven Development

  • The spec defines what to implement, abstractly, without line-by-line review.
  • Validates the idea before writing code; removes race conditions before production.
  • Brainstorm + spec can be 80% of the time; spec to execution plan ≈ 4 h. Then execution runs without friction.
  • A terminal multiplexer controls several agents, with subagents up to 4 levels deep.
Stage 02 · Execution

Parallel execution with audit

Each expert builds its scope; the auditor reviews and returns findings to whoever caused them.

The auditor checks
Adherence to specOut-of-scope changes · requirements · experts

2 · Experts per component

Spec→ Execute→ Curate→ PR
  • One expert for each major component of the repo: it keeps the non-obvious decisions in the code (why this API, this library…).
  • Orchestrator coordinates · Expert makes changes and logs · Auditor validates everything matches the spec, no extras.
  • Each expert has memory: logs are folded back in when the epic ends.

3 · PR review in 4 steps

  • Gate: classifies by size, impact and security; builds an impact graph.
  • Verify: lint, checks, automated tests.
  • Review: large model for sensitive PRs, light one for copy/labels. Separate pipelines for security and logic.
  • Human validates the review is coherent, approves and merges.

4 · Automated infra and QA

  • Son of Anton: VMs to develop and validate in parallel; one dev can have 5 changes running at once.
  • Maestro (nightly QA): Android, iOS and web flows every night; alerts if something fails.
  • Night Shift: every Wednesday scans vulnerable dependencies and opens a PR.
  • Sentry + agent: tries to fix prod errors; if it can't, assigns the diagnosis to whoever last touched the code.

Results they shared

  • Bugs: from ~5/week to 1–3/week, with very few recurrences.
  • Fewer PRs per epic, more focused and reviewable.
  • Costs: max out included subscriptions before paid APIs; orchestrator on a large model, subagents on small ones.
  • Stable frontend: experts read the design system and the design spec is very specific.

The engineer's role changes

  • Think product: why this button, how it looks in 3, 6 and 12 months.
  • Key skill: conveying context effectively to the LLM.
  • Be clear on the sequence of steps before delegating.
  • Keep coding to understand what the agent does. Infra still demands a lot of care.

What we can apply at Revyse

  • Invest more time in the spec before asking an agent for code.
  • Document non-obvious decisions per component as context for agents.
  • Resolve AI reviewer comments before human review.
  • PR pipeline by complexity: model by risk, security separate.
  • Try automated nightly QA and a weekly dependency scan.
  • Generate test cases with a context-free agent, given only the endpoint list.
